(2023). MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI. arXiv:2311.16502.
creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen (IN.AI Research, University of Waterloo, The Ohio State University, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Victoria, Princeton University)
description: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning) is a benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines (Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering) across 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.
name: MMMU
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question has one correct answer annotation. Questions with explanations (17.62% of the dataset, 2,035 questions) also include an explanation annotation.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in the 30 covered subjects served as annotators for data collection. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent a wide range of experts across the 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A secondary review team rigorously vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence. Regular audits of random samples from the dataset were conducted to ensure sustained quality and consistency. Ambiguities or unclear data instances were flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom web interface developed for data annotation and verification (developed by Tianyu Zheng as part of the project)
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators collected multimodal questions from free online resources, quizzes, textbooks, and other study materials. All questions must contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, and not be ambiguous. Questions were categorized as multiple-choice or open-ended. Annotators annotated all fields including question text, answer options, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation (if available). Data was stored in JSON format. Annotators were instructed to avoid questions with easily accessible answers and to select questions whose answers are in less obvious locations (e.g., separate documents or end of textbooks) to mitigate data contamination.
rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. The benchmark covers 30 subjects but excludes some subjects like law and linguistics because it was difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems in those areas. Annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers to mitigate data contamination concerns from foundation models.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected in three stages. First, 30 subjects from six disciplines were selected based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted. Second, over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in these majors were recruited as annotators to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks, online resources, and lecture materials, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations and to select questions without immediately available answers (e.g., answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks). This process resulted in a diverse collection of approximately 13K questions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions collected from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, online resources, and lecture materials across 30 subjects and 6 disciplines. The raw collection comprised approximately 13K questions before quality filtering.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and "90th percentile of skilled adults," nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. Some subjects like law and linguistics were excluded due to difficulty finding enough relevant multimodal problems.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two-stage data cleaning was performed: (1) Lexical overlap and source URL similarity were used to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications. (2) Problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format. In a third stage, authors categorized problems into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard), and approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MMMU is designed to monitor progress towards Expert AGI, which is defined as AI reaching "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks. Achieving Expert AGI could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The benchmark aims to provide a rigorous evaluation tool to track AI capabilities and stimulate development of next-generation multimodal foundation models.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating multimodal foundation models on expert-level college-level multi-discipline understanding and reasoning tasks. Benchmarking progress towards Expert AGI. Assessing LMMs' perception, knowledge, and reasoning capabilities across diverse disciplines. Stimulating development of next-generation multimodal foundation models.

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific dates or time period for data collection are mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data handling in the collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; the dataset consists of discrete QA items without missing value imputation.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation, augmentation, or resampling is described for the dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine annotation tools were used in the dataset annotation pipeline; all annotation was done manually by human annotators.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of college-level academic questions and images; no personal or sensitive information is collected. The annotation protocol explicitly states annotators should avoid collecting questions containing private information.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No formal versioning or maintenance plan is described, though the paper notes a live-updating leaderboard and version change log showing updates were made.
null_reasons.publisher: No single publishing organization is identified; the dataset is a collaborative effort across multiple universities (University of Waterloo, Ohio State University, etc.) and IN.AI Research.
null_reasons.license: No license is explicitly stated in the paper.
